categories.name: Qur’anic Studies
categories.description: Close readings of the Qur’anic passages cited in the Islamic Dilemma debate, in Arabic, in context and with the classical commentaries.

categories.name: Biblical Texts
categories.description: The Gospel, the New Testament and the history of the biblical text, read with Christian scholarship.

categories.name: Replies and Rejoinders
categories.description: Answers to the follow-up claims made alongside the Islamic Dilemma, about Islam, sin, salvation and the nature of God.

tags.name: 1 John 5:7
tags.definition: The Johannine Comma: a Trinitarian addition to 1 John 5:7–8 absent from the early Greek manuscripts and omitted by modern critical editions.

tags.name: Ahl al-Kitāb
tags.definition: The People of the Book: Jews and Christians, addressed in the Qur'an.

tags.name: Aḥruf
tags.definition: The modes in which the Qur'an was revealed, allowing recitation in more than one form.

tags.name: al-Fārūqī
tags.definition: Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī (1921–1986), Palestinian-American philosopher and scholar of comparative religion; author of *Al Tawḥīd: Its Implications for Thought and Life*.

tags.name: al-Zabūr
tags.definition: The revelation given to David, usually understood as the Psalms {Q 4:163}.

tags.name: Answering Islam
tags.definition: A Christian polemical website, where the Islamic Dilemma was first set out in English.

tags.name: Atonement
tags.definition: The Christian doctrine that Christ's death pays for the sins of others. The Qur'an teaches that no soul bears another's burden {Q 53:38}.

tags.name: Āya
tags.definition: A verse of the Qur'an; also a sign.

tags.name: Canon
tags.definition: The list of books a community accepts as scripture.

tags.name: Classical scholarship
tags.definition: The commentary and theology of the early and medieval Muslim scholars, such as al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī and Ibn Kathīr, read in their own terms.

tags.name: Codex Sinaiticus
tags.definition: A fourth-century Greek Bible, the only complete fourth-century New Testament. It includes the Epistle of Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas.

tags.name: Comma Johanneum
tags.definition: The 'three witnesses in heaven' of 1 John 5:7, absent from the early Greek manuscripts.

tags.name: Crucifixion
tags.definition: The death of Jesus on the cross, affirmed in the Gospels and denied in Q 4:157 in the form the verse describes.

tags.name: Ḍaʿīf
tags.definition: Weak: a hadith with a defect in its chain or text.

tags.name: David Wood
tags.definition: American Christian apologist who put the Islamic Dilemma into the form of a syllogism, through Acts 17 Apologetics and Answering Muslims.

tags.name: Dawah
tags.definition: *Daʿwa*: the invitation to Islam, made by speech, reasoning and example.

tags.name: Dead Sea Scrolls
tags.definition: Manuscripts found in the caves near Qumran between 1946 and 1956, copied between about 250 BCE and 68 CE.

tags.name: Diatessaron
tags.definition: Tatian's single Gospel woven from the four, c. 170 CE, used in the Syriac churches for centuries.

tags.name: Dīn al-ḥanīf
tags.definition: The primordial religion of pure monotheism, taught by every prophet {Q 30:30}.

tags.name: Fiṭra
tags.definition: The natural disposition God places in every human to know Him.

tags.name: Forgiveness
tags.definition: God's pardon of sin. In Islam it comes through repentance, with no need for a sacrifice.

tags.name: Furqān
tags.definition: Criterion, that which separates truth from falsehood. Applied to the Qur'an and also to the revelation given to Moses.

tags.name: Gospel of John
tags.definition: The fourth Gospel, the one most often cited for the divinity of Jesus.

tags.name: Guidance
tags.definition: *Hidāya*: God's direction of a person to the truth, which He gives to whom He wills.

tags.name: Hadith
tags.definition: A report of the words or actions of the Prophet, preserved through a chain of narrators.

tags.name: Ḥasan
tags.definition: Good: a grade just below sound.

tags.name: Ḥawāriyyūn
tags.definition: The disciples of Jesus, who declared themselves helpers in God's cause {Q 3:52}.

tags.name: Hebrews 9:22
tags.definition: “Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.” Cited as the foundation of the case that Jesus had to die.

tags.name: Injil
tags.definition: The revelation God gave Jesus. Always singular in the Qur'an; not the four Gospels.

tags.name: Irenaeus
tags.definition: Bishop of Lyon, writing around 180. The first Christian author known to defend a fourfold Gospel canon formally.

tags.name: Isnād
tags.definition: The chain of narrators by which a hadith is transmitted.

tags.name: Jesus
tags.definition: ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, the Messiah, a messenger of God in the Qur'an. The central figure of the Gospels.

tags.name: John 14:6
tags.definition: “I am the way, the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” Cited for exclusive salvation.

tags.name: John 20:28
tags.definition: Thomas says to the risen Jesus, “My Lord and my God!” Cited for the deity of Jesus.

tags.name: Love of God
tags.definition: God's love for His servants, taught in both traditions, and the question of how each describes it.

tags.name: Mark 8:31
tags.definition: The first of Jesus' predictions of his suffering, death and resurrection in Mark. Cited as evidence that he foretold the cross.

tags.name: Masoretic Text
tags.definition: The standard Hebrew text, fixed by Jewish scholars between about the 7th and 10th centuries.

tags.name: Matthew 23
tags.definition: Jesus' address against the scribes and Pharisees. Verses 2–3 tell the crowds to do what those who sit on Moses' seat say, but not what they do.

tags.name: Mercy
tags.definition: *Raḥma*: the mercy of God, which Islam places at the head of His names and every sūra but one.

tags.name: Method
tags.definition: How an argument is built and tested: the standards applied to each side, and whether they are the same.

tags.name: Muhaymin
tags.definition: Guardian, witness, trusted arbiter. The Qur'an's description of itself over the earlier books {Q 5:48}.

tags.name: Muṣaddiq
tags.definition: One who attests the truth of what came before. Used of the Qur'an, and of Jesus confirming the Torah.

tags.name: Muṣḥaf
tags.definition: A bound copy of the Qur'an.

tags.name: Nabī
tags.definition: A prophet. Muslims hold there was none between Jesus and Muhammad.

tags.name: Paul
tags.definition: Apostle to the Gentiles, to whom the New Testament ascribes thirteen letters. His authority is a premise of the Islamic Dilemma.

tags.name: People of the Book
tags.definition: *Ahl al-Kitāb*: Jews and Christians, the communities that received earlier scriptures.

tags.name: Pericope adulterae
tags.definition: The story of the woman taken in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, absent from the earliest manuscripts.

tags.name: Peshitta
tags.definition: The Syriac Bible. Its New Testament has 22 books.

tags.name: Preservation
tags.definition: The question of how a scripture's text has been kept and handed down, for the Qur'an and for the Bible.

tags.name: Pseudepigraphy
tags.definition: Writing under another person's name. Most scholars think several letters in Paul's name are pseudepigraphic.

tags.name: Q 10:94
tags.definition: “If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, ask those who have been reading the Book before you.” Used by the Islamic Dilemma to claim that the Qur'an sends the Prophet to the Bible.

tags.name: Q 112:3
tags.definition: “He neither begets nor is begotten.” From Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ, on the oneness of God.

tags.name: Q 15:9
tags.definition: “We sent down the Reminder, and We will guard it.” The verse most cited for the preservation of the Qur'an.

tags.name: Q 18:27
tags.definition: Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord. None can change His words. The verse speaks of the Qur'an itself.

tags.name: Q 19:28
tags.definition: Mary's people address her as “sister of Aaron”, which critics read as confusing her with Miriam. The phrase is an address of lineage and piety.

tags.name: Q 19:30
tags.definition: The infant Jesus speaks in the cradle: “I am the servant of God. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet.”

tags.name: Q 19:88
tags.definition: “They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a son.’” The Qur'an denies that God takes a son in any sense.

tags.name: Q 2:136
tags.definition: “We believe in God and in what was revealed to us, and to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes, and what Moses and Jesus were given.” The Muslim declaration of faith in all the prophets.

tags.name: Q 2:23
tags.definition: The challenge to those who doubt the revelation: produce a sūra like it, and call on any witnesses besides God.

tags.name: Q 2:255
tags.definition: Āyat al-Kursī, the Throne Verse: God is the Living, the Self-Sustaining; neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him.

tags.name: Q 2:75
tags.definition: Asks whether the Prophet's hearers can hope that certain Jews, who heard the word of God and then distorted it knowingly, will believe. One of four verses with the verb *yuḥarrifūna*, “they distort”.

tags.name: Q 2:85
tags.definition: Rebukes those who believe part of the Book and reject part. The Islamic Dilemma reads it as a rule for Muslims; the commentators read it as a charge against a particular group's conduct.

tags.name: Q 29:46
tags.definition: Argue with the People of the Book only in the best way, and say: “We believe in what was sent down to us and to you; our God and your God is one.”

tags.name: Q 3:185
tags.definition: “Every soul will taste death.” Every person is repaid in full on the Day of Resurrection.

tags.name: Q 3:50
tags.definition: Jesus says he confirms the Torah before him and makes lawful some of what had been forbidden. The Qur'an's own model of *taṣdīq*.

tags.name: Q 3:84
tags.definition: “We make no distinction between any of them.” A declaration of belief in all the prophets and the revelations they received.

tags.name: Q 4:157
tags.definition: The verse on the crucifixion: “they did not kill him, and they did not crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them.”

tags.name: Q 4:171
tags.definition: Addresses the People of the Book: do not exceed the limits of your religion. The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was only a messenger of God and His word.

tags.name: Q 4:46
tags.definition: Certain Jews shift words from their places. Al-Ṭabarī and others read this as distortion of meaning and of speech, not of the written text.

tags.name: Q 4:82
tags.definition: Asks whether people reflect on the Qur'an, and states that, had it come from other than God, they would have found much discrepancy in it.

tags.name: Q 5:116
tags.definition: God asks Jesus whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods besides God. Jesus answers that he said only what he was commanded: worship God.

tags.name: Q 5:13
tags.definition: God took a covenant from the Children of Israel; because they broke it, they shift words from their places and forget part of what they were told.

tags.name: Q 5:43
tags.definition: Asks why some of the Prophet's hearers come to him for judgment when they have the Torah, which contains God's ruling. Opens the passage 5:43–48 on legal judgment.

tags.name: Q 5:46
tags.definition: God sent Jesus, confirming the Torah before him, and gave him the Gospel, which holds guidance and light.

tags.name: Q 5:47
tags.definition: “Let the people of the Gospel judge by what God has revealed therein.” Read as a command in most canonical readings, and as a statement in others.

tags.name: Q 5:48
tags.definition: God sent down the Book to the Prophet confirming (*muṣaddiq*) the Book before it and as *muhaymin* over it: a witness, a trustee and a judge.

tags.name: Q 5:68
tags.definition: “You have no standing until you uphold the Torah, the Gospel and what has been sent down to you from your Lord.” A call to the People of the Book to act on their scriptures.

tags.name: Q 5:75
tags.definition: The Messiah, son of Mary, was only a messenger; messengers had passed before him. He and his mother ate food.

tags.name: Q 50:38
tags.definition: God created the heavens and the earth in six days, and no weariness touched Him. A reply to the idea that God rested.

tags.name: Q 53:36–39
tags.definition: Speaks of what is in the scrolls (*ṣuḥuf*) of Moses and Abraham: no soul bears the burden of another, and a person has only what he strives for.

tags.name: Q 57:27
tags.definition: God gave Jesus the Gospel and put compassion and mercy in the hearts of his followers. Monasticism they invented; God did not prescribe it.

tags.name: Q 6:115
tags.definition: The word of your Lord is complete in truth and justice. There is no changing His words.

tags.name: Q 7:157
tags.definition: Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel.

tags.name: Q 87:18–19
tags.definition: This is in the earlier scrolls, the scrolls of Abraham and Moses.

tags.name: Qira’at
tags.definition: The recognised readings of the Qur'an, each traced to the Prophet, differing in vowels, dots and a few words.

tags.name: Qur’an
tags.definition: The Book revealed to the Prophet Muḥammad, recited and written down, and the central scripture of Islam.

tags.name: Qur’anic exegesis
tags.definition: *Tafsīr*: the commentary tradition that explains the Qur'an verse by verse.

tags.name: Rajm
tags.definition: Stoning, the penalty for adultery in the Torah and in the hadith about the Jews of Medina.

tags.name: Rasūl
tags.definition: A messenger: a prophet who brings a scripture.

tags.name: Reason
tags.definition: *ʿAql*: the faculty by which a person weighs evidence and arguments, which the Qur'an repeatedly asks its hearers to use.

tags.name: Reconsidering the Islamic Dilemma
tags.definition: The 2026 study by Mohd Elfie Nieshaem Juferi on which this site is based.

tags.name: Ṣaḥīḥ
tags.definition: Sound: the highest grade for a hadith. Also the title of the collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

tags.name: Sam Shamoun
tags.definition: Christian apologist who first set out the Islamic Dilemma in English, on the Answering Islam website.

tags.name: Samaritan Pentateuch
tags.definition: The five books of Moses as preserved by the Samaritans; one of three early witnesses to the text, with the Septuagint and the Masoretic Text.

tags.name: Septuagint
tags.definition: The Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, begun in the 3rd century BCE.

tags.name: Shahāda
tags.definition: The testimony of faith: 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God.'

tags.name: Ṣuḥuf
tags.definition: Scrolls. The Qur'an speaks of the scrolls of Abraham and Moses {Q 87:19}.

tags.name: Sūra
tags.definition: A chapter of the Qur'an. There are 114.

tags.name: Tafsīr
tags.definition: Commentary on the Qur'an. Major works include al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī.

tags.name: Taḥrīf
tags.definition: Distortion. Classically divided into distortion of wording (*lafẓ*) and of meaning (*maʿnā*).

tags.name: Taḥrīf al-lafẓ
tags.definition: Distortion of the wording of a text.

tags.name: Taḥrīf al-maʿnā
tags.definition: Distortion of the meaning, by misreading or explaining away.

tags.name: Taṣdīq
tags.definition: Confirmation: declaring true, verifying, putting right. Applied to a message or a prophet, not to a manuscript.

tags.name: Tawātur
tags.definition: Transmission by so many that collusion is impossible. The basis of the Qur'an's certain text.

tags.name: Tawḥīd
tags.definition: The oneness of God: the centre of Islam.

tags.name: Textual criticism
tags.definition: The study of manuscripts to work out what an original text said.

tags.name: Textual history
tags.definition: How a text was copied, transmitted and edited over time, and what the manuscripts show.

tags.name: Torah
tags.definition: The revelation given to Moses. Singular in the Qur'an; not a multi-book canon.

tags.name: Trinity
tags.definition: The Christian doctrine, formulated in the fourth century, that God is three persons in one being. The Qur'an rejects it {Q 4:171}.

tags.name: Uthmanic codex
tags.definition: The standard copy made under ʿUthmān around 650 CE, from which copies were sent to the major cities.
